## Teaching points

1. A spinal epidural hematoma can present as sudden hemiparesis within the thrombolysis window. Neck or back pain with weakness, especially on an anticoagulant, should raise the possibility.
2. Clues to a cord lesion: sensory loss with a level below the neck, sparing of the face and no cranial nerve signs; Brown-Séquard features, Lhermitte sign or an ipsilateral Horner syndrome may also occur.
3. Review the cervical spine on the code-stroke CT angiogram: an epidural hyperdense lesion can make the diagnosis before MRI.
4. Thrombolysis in spinal epidural hematoma is associated with deterioration; in a review cited by the authors, 10 of 13 thrombolysed patients worsened and 9 needed surgery.
5. Mild, non-progressive deficits can be managed conservatively; decompressive laminectomy is the standard for severe or worsening deficits.
